title: What is `collect()` vs `take(n)` vs `head(n)` vs `first()` — `collect()` brings ALL rows to the driver (dangerous on large data, causes driver OOM), `take(n)`/`head(n)` bring only n rows (bounded, safe), `first()` = `take(1)` — and why should you never `collect()` a large DataFrame?
shortTitle: collect() vs take(n) vs head(n) vs first()

s1_definition.profdef: These are Spark actions that pull rows from the distributed executors back to the single driver JVM. `collect()` brings the entire DataFrame to the driver as a list, which risks an out-of-memory crash on large data because all rows must fit in driver memory. `take(n)` and `head(n)` bring only the first n rows, so they are bounded and safe. `first()` is equivalent to `take(1)[0]`, returning a single row. You should never collect a large DataFrame because the driver has finite memory and gathering millions of rows there defeats the purpose of distributed processing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank's transactions are spread across many branch offices (executors), and the head office (driver) wants to look at them. `collect()` orders every branch to ship every single transaction to head office, which overflows the head office's small storage room and it collapses. `take(5)` and `head(5)` ask for just five transactions to eyeball, which fits easily. `first()` asks for just one. You never truck the entire bank's records into one small room.
s1_definition.oneliner: collect pulls all rows to the driver and can crash it; take(n) and head(n) safely pull only n; first() is take(1) — never collect a large DataFrame.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are Spark actions that pull rows from the distributed executors back to the single driver JVM. `collect()` brings the entire DataFrame to the driver as a list, which risks an out-of-memory crash on large data because all rows must fit in driver memory. `take(n)` and `head(n)` bring only the first n rows, so they are bounded and safe. `first()` is equivalent to `take(1)[0]`, returning a single row. You should never collect a large DataFrame because the driver has finite memory and gathering millions of rows there defeats the purpose of distributed processing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank's transactions are spread across many branch offices (executors), and the head office (driver) wants to look at them. `collect()` orders every branch to ship every single transaction to head office, which overflows the head office's small storage room and it collapses. `take(5)` and `head(5)` ask for just five transactions to eyeball, which fits easily. `first()` asks for just one. You never truck the entire bank's records into one small room.

**One line to remember:** collect pulls all rows to the driver and can crash it; take(n) and head(n) safely pull only n; first() is take(1) — never collect a large DataFrame.

sections.s2_technical:
Spark splits data across executors and processes it in parallel; the driver coordinates but has limited memory set by `spark.driver.memory`. Actions that return data to the driver must fit what they return in that memory.

`collect()` triggers execution and returns every row of the DataFrame to the driver as a local list. If the DataFrame has millions of rows or wide columns, the driver tries to hold all of it at once and throws an OutOfMemoryError, often after a long, expensive full computation. It should be reserved for small results you have deliberately reduced, such as an aggregate with a handful of rows.

`take(n)` returns the first n rows and is bounded: Spark reads partitions incrementally until it has n rows, so it does not compute or transfer the whole dataset. `head(n)` is the DataFrame equivalent and returns a list of n Row objects (head with no argument returns a single Row). `first()` returns the single first Row and is equivalent to `take(1)[0]`. These are the safe ways to peek at data or sanity-check a transformation.

The core guidance: never collect a large DataFrame. If you need all the data elsewhere, write it to storage with `df.write...` so the work stays distributed; if you need to inspect, use `show(n)`, `take(n)`, or `head(n)`; if you need an aggregate, compute it in Spark with `groupBy().agg()` and collect only the tiny result. For counting use `count()` rather than `len(collect())`.

A senior nuance: `show()` also brings rows to the driver but formats and limits them (default 20) and truncates columns, so it is safe for inspection; and `toLocalIterator()` streams rows to the driver one partition at a time, bounding memory when you genuinely must iterate a large result locally. Also beware that `collect` on a cached-but-huge DataFrame still materializes everything.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at the National Bank called collect on a full transactions DataFrame to count fraud cases, and the driver crashed with an out-of-memory error during month-end when volumes spiked. This is exactly the never-collect-large-data lesson.

Problem 2 — The right approach is to compute the aggregate in Spark and collect only the small summary, and to use take or head for quick inspection. This is exactly the safe-actions pattern.

Problem 3 — To move all data onward, write to storage rather than collecting. This demonstrates keeping work distributed.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`DriverActionsDemo`) that builds a large transactions DataFrame, shows safe `take`, `head`, and `first`, computes an aggregate collected safely, and contrasts with a clearly-labeled dangerous collect — for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) at scale.

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/driver_actions_demo.py
# Demonstrates safe driver actions vs dangerous collect for National Bank of India.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from inspect.safe_peek import SafePeek

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("DriverActionsDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("DriverActionsDemo")
            .config("spark.driver.memory", "1g").getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # 5 million transactions - too many to collect() into a 1g driver
    txns = spark.range(0, 5_000_000).select(
        F.concat(F.lit("TXN-"), F.col("id")).alias("txn_id"),
        F.when(F.col("id") % 2 == 0, F.lit("SAV2001")).otherwise(F.lit("CUR3001"))
            .alias("account_id"),
        (F.col("id") % 100000 + 1000).cast("double").alias("amount"))

    peek = SafePeek(txns)

    log.info("first() -> single Row: %s", peek.first_row())
    log.info("take(3) -> bounded list of 3 Rows:")
    for r in peek.take_rows(3):
        log.info("  %s", r)
    log.info("head(2) -> bounded list of 2 Rows:")
    for r in peek.head_rows(2):
        log.info("  %s", r)

    # SAFE: aggregate in Spark, collect only the TINY summary (2 rows)
    summary = peek.safe_summary()
    log.info("Safe aggregate summary (collected - only 2 rows):")
    for r in summary:
        log.info("  %s", r)

    # DANGEROUS (do NOT do this on large data): txns.collect()  -> driver OOM
    log.warning("Skipping txns.collect() - it would OOM the 1g driver")
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/inspect/safe_peek.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F, Row
from typing import List

class SafePeek:
    """Safe, bounded ways to look at and summarize a large DataFrame."""
    def __init__(self, df: DataFrame):
        self.df = df

    def first_row(self) -> Row:
        return self.df.first()                 # == take(1)[0], one row

    def take_rows(self, n: int) -> List[Row]:
        return self.df.take(n)                 # bounded: reads until n rows

    def head_rows(self, n: int) -> List[Row]:
        return self.df.head(n)                 # DataFrame equivalent of take(n)

    def safe_summary(self) -> List[Row]:
        # reduce in Spark FIRST, then collect only the small result
        return (self.df.groupBy("account_id")
                .agg(F.count("*").alias("cnt"), F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
                .collect())
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 5,000,000 synthetic transactions split across SAV2001 and CUR3001.

Step 1: `first()` triggers a minimal job that reads just enough of one partition to return a single Row, so the driver receives one row.

Step 2: `take(3)` reads partitions incrementally until it has three rows and returns them. It never scans the full five million, so it is bounded and cheap.

Step 3: `head(2)` behaves the same, returning two rows. Both are safe inspection tools.

Step 4: `safe_summary()` performs the reduction inside Spark: it groups by account and computes count and sum across the executors in parallel, producing only two result rows. Only those two tiny rows are collected to the driver, which fits easily in 1g.

Step 5: The code explicitly skips `txns.collect()` and logs a warning, because collecting five million rows into a 1g driver would throw an OutOfMemoryError. The correct way to move all data would be a distributed write.

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are all Spark actions that pull rows from the distributed executors back to the single driver JVM, and the whole point is how much they pull. collect brings the entire DataFrame to the driver as a local list, which is dangerous on large data because the driver has finite memory set by spark dot driver dot memory, so gathering millions of rows there throws an OutOfMemoryError, usually after an expensive full computation. take of n and head of n bring only the first n rows and are bounded, because Spark reads partitions incrementally until it has n rows rather than computing the whole dataset. first returns a single Row and is equivalent to take of one then index zero.

So the rule I follow is: never collect a large DataFrame. If I just want to peek at data or sanity-check a transformation, I use show, take, or head, which are bounded and safe. If I need a metric, I compute it inside Spark with groupBy and agg so the reduction happens in parallel on the executors, and I collect only the tiny summary, which might be a handful of rows. If I actually need all the data somewhere else, I write it to storage with df dot write so the work stays distributed and never funnels through the driver. For counting I use count rather than taking the length of a collect.

At the National Bank of India this was a real incident. A developer called collect on a full transactions DataFrame to count fraud cases, and during month-end when volumes spiked the driver ran out of memory and the job died. I rewrote it to compute the fraud count with a groupBy and agg in Spark and collect only the small result, and I used take and head for quick inspection during development. The nuances I mention are that show is safe because it limits and truncates, that toLocalIterator streams one partition at a time when I genuinely must iterate a large result locally, and that the golden rule remains: reduce in Spark, collect small, write large.
